Vance had laid his hands flat on the table before Miller entered. He kept them there while Miller sat down, as if the room had asked him to prove he had brought nothing in.

The interview room smelled of overheated dust and lemon cleaner. Miller set a paper cup of water between them. Vance looked at it but did not touch it.

“You said you saw me,” Miller said.

“I did.”

“Where?”

“In the room.”

“Which room?”

“The room where he died.”

Miller opened the thin folder. The first page held Vance’s statement, two paragraphs in a clerk’s typeface. The second held a photograph of the apartment’s narrow kitchen. A chair lay on its side near the sink. The light over the stove had been left on.

“You were there at what time?”

“After ten. I had the key because—” Vance stopped. He glanced at the recorder. “I already told the other detective.”

“Tell me.”

“I was supposed to pick up my coat. It was still there.”

Miller wrote that down, though it was already in the statement. “And you saw me?”

“By the stove.”

“What was I doing?”

Vance swallowed. His hands remained flat. “You were holding the knife.”

Miller waited. The ventilation fan clicked twice and settled into a low rattle.

“Did you see my face?”

“Yes.”

“From the doorway?”

“From the hall. The door was open.”

The photograph showed a kitchen doorway in the center of the frame. Miller moved it closer to Vance. “Stand up and show me where you were.”

“I don’t want to.”

“You can stay seated. Point.”

Vance lifted one finger and set it at the paper’s lower edge, just outside the doorway. “Here.”

“That’s the hall.”

“Yes.”

“The light in the kitchen was on?”

“Yes.”

“And you saw the knife?”

“Yes.”

“Which hand?”

Vance looked at his own right hand. “This one.”

Miller wrote the answer. He could feel the damp edge of his collar against his neck. He had come in from the rain, and the station’s heat had turned the collar cold.

“Did I look at you?”

“You looked right at me.”

“What did I say?”

“You told me to go.”

“Did I?”

Vance’s face tightened. “You were there.”

“I’m asking what you heard.”

“You told me to go.”

Miller leaned back. The chair gave a short squeak. “And what did you do?”

“I left.”

“Through the front door?”

“Yes.”

“The building camera shows you in the stairwell at ten twenty-three. It shows you entering the building at ten thirty-one.”

Vance stared at the cup.

“That’s eight minutes,” Miller said. “You told the first detective you were inside for less than a minute.”

“I was confused.”

“You remember my face. You remember which hand held the knife. You remember my exact words. But not the eight minutes.”

“I was scared.”

Miller closed the folder. “That makes sense.”

Vance looked up, wary of agreement.

“It still leaves a gap.”

“I didn’t kill him.”

“I haven’t asked whether you did.”

“You’re asking me about the camera like I—”

“I’m asking you about what you remember.”

Vance pressed his lips together. Outside the glass, a uniformed officer crossed the corridor carrying a stack of forms. The paper edges tapped against his sleeve with every step.

Miller opened the folder again. “You also said the kitchen clock read ten fourteen.”

“It did.”

“The photograph was taken at ten twelve.”

Vance’s finger moved a fraction. “The clock was fast.”

“How fast?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did you see it when you came in?”

“Yes.”

“Did it say ten fourteen then?”

“I think so.”

“Did you look at it before you saw me?”

Vance frowned. “I saw you first.”

“Then the clock.”

“Maybe.”

Miller let the silence sit. Questions could become noise if he stacked them too quickly. Vance watched his pencil, not his face.

“You had a reason to be in that apartment,” Miller said. “You went back for your coat. You saw something frightening. That may be all there is to it. But your statement has details that don’t fit the camera or the photograph.”

“I saw you.”

Miller felt the words land with the weight of a fact already accepted by someone else. “What were you wearing?”

Vance’s brow furrowed.

“When you saw me. What was I wearing?”

“A dark coat.”

“Was it wet?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did I have a badge?”

“I didn’t see.”

“A radio?”

“No.”

“Gloves?”

“I don’t remember.”

“You remember the knife, the hand, the face, and the words.”

“I know what I saw.”

Miller turned to the photograph. He had worn a dark coat that night. So had most of the detectives who went into the building. He had entered the apartment after the first patrol unit secured the hall. He had not held the knife. There was a report, a chain-of-custody log, and a partner who could confirm the hour. None of that told him what Vance had seen.

“Do you remember the knife’s handle?” Miller asked.

Vance looked at the photograph again. “Black.”

“It’s wood.”

“I thought it was black.”

“Did you see it clearly?”

Vance’s jaw moved. “I saw you holding it.”

Miller put the photo away. “I’m going to pause the interview.”

“You don’t believe me.”

“I believe you remember something. I don’t know yet whether the details arrived in the order you remember them.”

“That sounds like not believing me.”

“It sounds like keeping two things separate.”

He stopped the recorder. Vance’s shoulders lowered, but only a little. Miller gathered the pages without standing.

At the door, Vance said, “You’ll ask the others?”

Miller turned back.

“They all saw something different,” Vance said. “That’s why you’re asking me.”

Miller had not told him that.

“Who told you about the others?”

“No one.”

The answer might have been true. It might have been a guess. Miller looked at Vance’s hands, still flat on the table, and then at the empty cup.

He restarted the recorder. “Tell me what you mean by ‘the others.’”

Vance stared at the red light. “They remember the murder differently.”

Miller sat back down. The fan clicked twice overhead. The folder remained open between them, the photograph hidden beneath the statement.

The bell over the front door rang while the kitchen timer was still counting down.

She was scraping burned sugar from the bottom of a saucepan when the sound reached her. One hand kept the pan steady. The other dragged the spoon across the blackened edge. The dining room beyond the pass had gone quiet in the particular way a room went quiet when a table noticed the kitchen had stopped moving.

“Two minutes,” called someone from the floor.

“I heard it.”

She set the pan down and wiped her hand on her apron. Opening night had already asked for more than the room could hold: a supplier who arrived late, a burner that sputtered, a table that ordered the same dish three different ways. The restaurant was small enough that every problem could be heard by everyone.

The bell rang again.

She pushed through the swinging door. A man stood just inside, rain stippling his jacket. For a moment she recognized only the shape of his shoulders. Then he turned toward the light.

Her brother.

He looked older than the last time she had seen him, though she could not have said what made it so. His hair was shorter. His hands were empty. The dining room’s chalkboard menu reflected in the wet sleeve of his jacket.

“What are you doing here?” she asked.

“I saw the lights.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No.” He glanced at the tables. “I know.”

Someone at the nearest table stopped pretending not to listen. She stepped closer to the door, keeping her voice low.

“Are you here to eat?”

“I can, if there’s room.”

“You can see there isn’t.”

“I can stand.”

“That’s not what I meant.”

He looked past her toward the kitchen. “You’re busy.”

“Very.”

“I’m not going to make a scene.”

“You’ve made it into one by walking through that door.”

The bell above them trembled in the draft and fell still. Her brother rubbed water from his palm onto his jeans. He had come without an umbrella. She noticed the small practical details because the alternative was to answer the question she did not want to ask: why tonight?

“Do you have work?” he said.

She searched his face. “What?”

“I’m looking for work. I thought maybe—”

“You thought maybe I’d hire you on opening night?”

“I thought you might need help.”

“I need a cook who knows the menu.”

“I can learn it.”

“Tonight?”

“I can wash dishes.”

She looked at the ticket rail through the pass. Three orders had appeared while she was away. A pan clanged. The timer began to chirp. Someone called her name from inside the kitchen.

“You can’t come back here,” she said.

“I wasn’t asking to.”

“You’re asking for a job.”

“I’m asking if you have one.”

The answer she wanted to give was simple. No. The answer she owed the dining room was simpler: get the orders out, keep the burners lit, do not turn one family argument into the evening’s entertainment.

She opened the door, then stopped with her hand on its brass handle.

“What can you do?”

“Wash dishes. Carry boxes. Prep vegetables.”

“Can you follow a list without changing it?”

“Yes.”

“Can you show up when I tell you to?”

His eyes shifted. “Yes.”

“Can you leave when I tell you to?”

“I can.”

The timer kept chirping. She shut it off from across the room. In the kitchen, a cook lifted a pan from the flame and waited for her instruction.

“Two minutes,” she called, then to her brother: “There’s a sink. You can wash until the dinner rush eases. No knives, no stove. You don’t touch food. I’ll pay you for the hours. This is not a promise of another shift.”

He nodded once. “Okay.”

“Apron’s on the hook.”

“I remember.”

“You remember the hook?”

“The hook. The apron. The place.”

She felt the old reply rise, then let it pass. “Wash your hands first. There’s soap by the sink.”

He took off his jacket and hung it on the peg beside the door. For a second she noticed the carefulness of the gesture, the way he had chosen the outer peg rather than the one nearest hers. Then she went back through the swinging door.

The kitchen swallowed them. A cook handed her a plate. She tasted the sauce, added salt, and called the next order. Her brother found the apron and tied it at his waist. He went to the sink without asking where the detergent was.

The first stack of dishes was mostly glasses. He washed them slowly, turning each one under the tap and checking the rim. She set a bus tub beside him.

“Plates first,” she said. “The glasses can wait.”

“All right.”

“Scrape them into the bin. Don’t soak the tickets.”

“I won’t.”

She left him to it. The rush resumed around them, and for the next half hour the only exchange between them was practical. A clean plate. A request for more towels. A pan slid into the rack.

At the pass, a server whispered, “Is that your brother?”

She kept her eyes on the food. “He’s washing dishes.”

“That’s what I asked.”

“It’s what I answered.”

The server carried the plates away.

When the rush thinned, she found her brother still at the sink. His sleeves were rolled up. The apron was too short at the sides, the ties knotted twice. The tub was nearly empty.

“You don’t have to finish all of those,” she said.

“I said I’d wash.”

“You said you’d wash until the rush eased.”

“I’m almost done.”

She leaned against the counter. “Why tonight?”

He rinsed a bowl. “I didn’t know how else to ask.”

“You could have called.”

“I did.”

“When?”

“Last week.”

Her hand tightened around the edge of the counter. She remembered an unknown number and a voicemail she had deleted while checking a delivery. Or perhaps she did not.

“I didn’t get it,” she said.

“I figured.”

He set the bowl in the rack. The water ran over his wrists.

“I’m not asking you to forgive me,” he said.

“I didn’t ask you to.”

“I’m asking for a shift.”

“And if I say no next week?”

“Then I’ll look somewhere else.”

She watched him reach for another plate. There was no promise in the gesture, no proof that he would stay, and no reason she had to trust him because he had arrived wet and willing to work. The dining room still needed its tables wiped. Tomorrow still had to be planned.

“Finish the plates,” she said. “Then we’ll talk about next week when it’s actually next week.”

He nodded. She returned to the pass.

The bell above the front door rang again as a late customer entered. Her brother glanced up, then back to the sink. She called the order, and the kitchen moved around her.

They set the key on the table. It made a small, bright sound against the wood.

They went back to the table and picked up the key. It was no warmer now.

Their first turn had opened the lock. They put the key in again and turned it the other way. The mechanism moved without resistance. They tested the handle. This time it gave.

They did not decide what that meant.

The report was sealed in a gray envelope with a date fourteen days ahead.

Nia Calder checked the date on her phone, then the date on the envelope. The second looked too neat to be a copying mistake. It had been stamped by the municipal archive, in the same blue ink used for records that had already survived three offices and two audits.

She slit the envelope with a ruler.

Inside, the incident report described a seawall pump failure at the south intake. The report listed the pump’s serial number, the maintenance crew, and a time of day. The date was still two weeks away. The final paragraph said the failure would send water through the lower service corridor and close the harbor road until repairs were complete.

Nia read the page again, slower. The paper smelled of dust and wet stone. She checked the seal, the staple holes, the archive number. Nothing in the file said it was a forecast. It was formatted as an incident report, complete with a signature line and a blank space for the official who would have reviewed it.

She had not seen the file in yesterday’s inventory. The box listed reports from the current week; the envelope had no place among them. She wrote down its location before moving it: cabinet 4B, shelf three, behind the harbor permits.

The office phone rang. Nia let it ring twice while she opened the records database. The report number returned no match. She tried the pump serial number. One entry appeared, a maintenance schedule last updated nine months earlier. The pump existed. The failure did not.

She answered the phone.

“Archive desk,” she said.

A burst of static, then a woman asked for the east quay permits. Nia gave the caller the request form and tried not to look at the date on the envelope. The call lasted less than a minute. When she hung up, she opened the security camera feed.

The archive corridor was empty. The front entrance showed a courier delivering a stack of boxes. The loading door showed no movement. Nothing on the screen explained how a sealed file had arrived in a cabinet that had not appeared on the inventory.

A sound came from the reading room: a door latch settling.

Nia stood. She left the report on the desk and took the long way around the stacks. The reading room door was closed. Through its narrow glass panel, she could see the tables and the empty chairs. A drop of water marked the carpet just inside the threshold.

She turned back toward the office.

The cabinet doors stood open. A second gray envelope lay where the first had been, its seal split cleanly down one edge. A figure in a dark hood moved between the shelves, carrying the file box under one arm.

“Stop!”

The figure looked back. The face was covered. Nia could see one pale hand around the box and the other pressed against the wall to steady a quick turn.

“You can’t take those.”

The intruder ran for the side exit. Nia followed, the floor slick beneath her shoes. She reached the door just as it swung shut. The alarm gave a delayed chirp, a small electronic complaint, and the latch locked behind the figure.

Nia pressed the release and stepped into the service alley. Rain had blown in under the overhang. The alley split around a concrete ramp, and the hooded figure was already gone.

She returned to the cabinet. The second envelope was missing. The first remained open on the desk, the predicted pump failure laid bare beneath the fluorescent lights.

Nia called security and reported the theft. When the guard asked what had been taken, she said “a future-dated file.” He asked her to repeat it.

She wrote a statement before anyone could suggest another phrase. She recorded the envelope’s seal, the report number, the time she had found it, and the moment the masked person left with the second file. She did not write that the report was impossible. She did not write that it was a prediction. Those were explanations, and she had no evidence for either.

The incident form asked whether she knew the intruder’s identity. Nia checked no.

At the end of the day, she carried a copy of the pump serial number to the maintenance office. The clerk searched the work orders and found nothing scheduled for that date. Nia asked whether the pump had shown unusual readings.

“Not that I know of,” he said. “Why?”

“I’m checking an old report.”

He looked at her copy. The date sat between them, too far ahead to be ordinary and too precise to ignore.

Back at the archive, Nia locked the surviving envelope in the evidence cabinet. She could not ask the city to shut down the seawall on the basis of a page that did not exist in the database. She could verify the pump, compare the serial number, and see whether the report’s details matched the actual intake.

In her notebook she wrote: inspect south pump; request maintenance logs; preserve the envelope; ask for camera backup.

Then she added a final line: find the person who took the second report.

Outside the archive windows, the city’s harbor lights appeared one by one through the rain. Nia shut her notebook and left the report sealed behind the cabinet door. She still did not know why the page described an event that had not happened, or why someone had risked a break-in to steal another one.

The pump failure had a date. The Lantern had a file. For now, those were the facts she could carry forward.

The certificate had been signed three days from now.

Mara held it beneath the archive lamp. The name at the bottom belonged to Elias Vale, the records clerk who had vanished on Monday. The ink was dry. The date was not.

Jo leaned over the table without touching the seal. He had worked beside Elias for eleven years.

"Are you Mara Venn?" she asked.

Mara nodded.

"I am Sister Beatrice. Elias said you might look for him here."

Jo stood. "He said he had no family at the convent."

"He does not," Beatrice said. "The convent belongs to no one now. The roof belongs to the weather, and the west wall belongs to the sea."

She slid the key toward Mara. Its paper tag read ST. ORRA in Elias's narrow hand.

"Why bring this to me?" Mara asked.

"The archive sent a notice that the convent's death register had been transferred here. It has not. I checked."

Jo looked at the key. "What is at St. Orra?"

"Beds for people whose names were removed from the city rolls. People who need somewhere to sleep while the city argues whether they exist."

Mara turned the certificate over. A shelf mark had been pressed into the paper without ink. It matched the old convent's register.

Beatrice read it and went still. "That book is supposed to be empty."

Rain tapped the archive windows. Mara slipped the certificate into an evidence sleeve. She left the key where Beatrice had placed it.

"Show me the register," she said.

Beatrice glanced toward the locked archive door. "At low tide, the road is passable."

The certificate lay between them, dated three days ahead. No one reached for the key.

Mateo spread the seawall plans across the hood of his truck and held the corners down with two chipped mugs. Wind came off the harbor in short, cold bursts. Nia stood on the other side of the paper, one hand on the report sleeve in her coat pocket.

The pump sat below them in a concrete chamber behind the south intake. From the road, it looked ordinary: a squat green housing, a grated vent, and a ladder bolted to the seawall. The report had named its serial number and predicted a failure in fourteen days. Mateo had checked the number twice. It was the right pump.

"The plans say this intake was rebuilt in 1988," he said. "The report describes the old pressure bypass. That was removed before I was born."

"Could the failure still happen?"

"The current system can fail. I am not saying it cannot. I am saying the report names a part that is not here."

He traced a blue line toward the harbor wall. The line stopped at a small square stamped with a symbol like a lantern: three short rays over a narrow door. Nia knew it from the second file the intruder had taken. She had seen the same mark on the corner of the sealed report, faint beneath the archive stamp.

"That is not a pump mark," Mateo said. "It is on the relocation sheet too."

The relocation sheet had been folded into the plans and signed by a clerk whose office no longer existed. It listed crates moved from the old municipal forecasting office to the lower harbor, then marked as returned. The return date was blank.

Nia photographed the sheet and wrote the inventory number in her notebook. It could mean equipment. It could mean paper. It did not tell her why a report about a future failure used a removed bypass, or why someone had stolen another page with the same mark.

They followed the line on foot to a service lane behind the seawall. The old route ended at a bricked-up loading door. A newer path curved around the hill toward Saint Orra, where one wing of the former convent still had a working roof. Nia had passed the building before without noticing its stone lintel. The door stood open a handspan.

A woman inside was stacking ledgers on a table. She wore a dark cardigan over a plain collar and had tied her hair with a strip of blue cloth. When Nia knocked, the woman looked first at Mateo's municipal badge, then at the plan.

"We are looking for the old forecasting-office symbol," Nia said. "It appears on a seawall relocation record."

The woman did not answer at once. Behind her, the maintained wing held a narrow kitchen, two small rooms, and shelves of paper. The rest of the convent beyond a canvas partition was dark. Rain ticked through a hole in the outer roof and fell into a bucket.

"People come here asking about that mark when they want a machine to explain a human decision," the woman said.

"I want to know what was moved through the loading door."

"Then you want the ledgers, not a machine."

She introduced herself as Sister Beatrice and set a book on the table. Its cover had no title. The pages were crowded with names, dates, addresses, and short notes about families moved when the harbor district was cleared for redevelopment. It was not a municipal register. Some entries had no surname; others were crossed out and written again in a different hand.

Beatrice turned to a page marked with the same three rays over a narrow door. She said the symbol had been painted on the side of crates brought through the convent's lower entrance years earlier. Municipal workers had moved sealed equipment in after dark. She had been younger then, helping record which residents needed a bed while their homes were inspected. No one had told her what the crates contained.

"Did you see the equipment?" Mateo asked.

"I saw covered shapes and a trolley with a broken wheel. I heard a motor once. That is all I can say."

Nia checked the year against the relocation sheet. It matched. The page offered a non-governmental record of the movement, but it did not establish what the equipment did. She copied the ledger reference and asked Beatrice whether the book could be photographed.

"Not the names," Beatrice said. "Those people trusted me with where they slept. You can write down the crate mark. You can say I remember workers and covered equipment. Do not turn a shelter list into evidence about a machine."

Nia put her phone away. "Understood."

Mateo returned to the plan. The harbor equipment might connect the old office to the pump district, but the ledger could not confirm the report's prediction. He said he would inspect the current bypass and request the maintenance log. Nia wrote both actions beside the ledger reference.

Outside, the weather had worsened. A delivery van crawled along the hill and turned toward the harbor. Its rear doors were shut. A small white sticker on the bumper showed three rays above a narrow door.

Nia watched until the van disappeared below the wall. She did not call it the Lantern's vehicle or the city's equipment. She wrote down the plate and the time.

The future report still described a part the pump no longer had. The ledger placed sealed equipment near the harbor, years ago, without saying what it was. Sister Beatrice had given them a witness and a boundary: the records could support the movement of crates, not their purpose.

Nia folded the copy of the plan along its old creases. The pump needed checking. The symbol needed tracing. The explanation could wait for evidence.
